title: Bitches Brew
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: The record that made fusion a commercial and critical event. Thirteen musicians, three keyboards, two drummers, and Teo Macero assembling the released tracks from tape splices after the fact.
listenFor: The harmony barely moves for twenty minutes at a time. What changes is density and texture — musicians entering and dropping out — and the editing that Macero imposed afterwards.

title: In a Silent Way
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: Quieter and stranger than Bitches Brew, and the first place the electric approach fully works. Two side-long pieces built by Macero from short takes, with Tony Williams playing only the hi-hat for long stretches.
listenFor: The opening and closing sections of the title suite are the same take, used twice. Macero built the record's shape in the edit, and Davis approved it.
startTrack: In a Silent Way / It's About That Time

title: Heavy Weather
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: Fusion at its most melodically generous, with Jaco Pastorius in the band and 'Birdland' as an actual hit. The group had a rule that everyone soloed all the time and nobody soloed, and you can hear it work.
listenFor: Pastorius plays fretless electric bass with harmonics and a singing tone that had no precedent. On 'Teen Town' he plays bass and drums both.

title: The Inner Mounting Flame
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: The loudest, fastest and most technically aggressive fusion band, playing odd meters at rock volume with a distorted guitar and an amplified violin. It genuinely frightened people in 1971.
listenFor: 'Dance of Maya' moves between 20/8 and a shuffle blues. Count the opening and you will fail; feel it and it works.

title: Romantic Warrior
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: Fusion's most unembarrassed virtuoso record, with a medieval concept and playing of frightening precision. It is the high-water mark of the technique-forward wing and the point where the backlash became inevitable.
listenFor: Everything is executed in unison at speed — guitar, bass and keyboard playing the same intricate line. The ensemble precision is the achievement, not the solos.

title: Emergency!
label: Polydor
whyThisOne: Recorded months before Bitches Brew and considerably more violent. Organ, distorted guitar and Williams playing at full volume, badly recorded, and all the better for it.
listenFor: The recording is genuinely poor — distorted and muddy — and the band plays through it. This is jazz musicians choosing rock's volume without rock's production.

title: On the Corner
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: Reviled on release and now treated as prophetic. It is an unbroken funk machine with tabla and sitar, aimed explicitly at a young Black audience that Davis felt he had lost.
listenFor: The bass line barely changes for the whole record and the trumpet is buried in the mix. Davis is making a groove record, and the soloing is a texture inside it.

title: Jaco Pastorius
label: Epic
whyThisOne: A debut that reintroduced the electric bass as a lead instrument, covering Charlie Parker, playing solo bass with harmonics, and putting a soul vocal duo on a jazz record.
listenFor: 'Portrait of Tracy' is solo fretless bass played almost entirely in artificial harmonics. Nobody had made the instrument sound like that.

title: Third
label: CBS
whyThisOne: The British route into fusion, coming from psychedelic rock rather than from jazz. Four side-long pieces, tape loops, fuzz organ, and a rhythmic approach that owes more to minimalism than to funk.
listenFor: 'Out-Bloody-Rageous' opens with tape loops that predate most electronic jazz by two decades. The Canterbury scene arrived at fusion independently.

title: Head Hunters
label: Columbia
whyThisOne: Hancock deliberately built a band around a groove rather than around soloing, and it became one of the best-selling jazz albums ever made. Everything in jazz-funk after this is measured against it.
listenFor: 'Chameleon' is one bass line for fifteen minutes. The clavinet and the synth bass do all the harmonic work and nothing modulates.

title: Black Byrd
label: Blue Note
whyThisOne: Blue Note's best-selling album of all time at the point of release, produced by the Mizell brothers with a hard bop trumpeter in front. It was treated as a betrayal at the time and has been mined by producers ever since.
listenFor: Byrd's trumpet is one colour among many; the arrangement, the vocal harmonies and the bass line are the composition. That inversion is what upset the critics.

title: Everybody Loves the Sunshine
label: Polydor
whyThisOne: The title track is one of the most sampled recordings in existence, and the album around it is a study in doing almost nothing with total conviction.
listenFor: The title track has essentially two chords and a mist of Rhodes and vibraphone. The mood is the content, and it is why hip-hop producers kept returning to it.

title: Swiss Movement
label: Atlantic
whyThisOne: Recorded at Montreux in 1969 by musicians who had barely rehearsed, and 'Compared to What' became a protest anthem. It is jazz-funk before the studio production arrived.
listenFor: Eddie Harris is playing an electrified tenor through a Varitone attachment. The horn's processed tone is a deliberate technological choice, not a studio effect.

artist: Lonnie Liston Smith and the Cosmic Echoes
title: Expansions
label: Flying Dutchman
whyThisOne: The bridge between spiritual jazz and the dancefloor: modal, echoing, mystical, and built on a bass line that London DJs were still playing fifteen years later.
listenFor: The title track's bass figure and the electric piano wash. This is the specific sound that acid jazz set out to recreate.

title: Root Down
label: Verve
whyThisOne: The organ pioneer, live in Los Angeles in 1972, playing over a hard funk rhythm section rather than a swing one. The Beastie Boys built a track around it two decades later.
listenFor: Smith's vocabulary has not changed since 1958; the rhythm section underneath it has changed completely. That is the whole soul-jazz-to-jazz-funk transition in one record.

title: Two
label: CTI
whyThisOne: Historically important for a reason James did not intend: 'Take Me to the Mardi Gras' contains a bell-and-drum break that became one of hip-hop's foundational samples.
listenFor: The break at the start of 'Take Me to the Mardi Gras' — sleigh bells and drums — turns up in dozens of rap records. Here it is, in context, doing nothing much.
startTrack: Take Me to the Mardi Gras

title: Harlem Bush Music – Taifa
label: Milestone
whyThisOne: Bartz had just left Miles Davis and made a record with chanted Swahili, political text and a groove. It sits precisely between spiritual jazz's intent and jazz-funk's body.
listenFor: Andy Bey's voice is used as an instrument in unison with the alto, and the material is explicitly about Black self-determination rather than about transcendence.

title: Power of Soul
label: Kudu
whyThisOne: A New Orleans drummer leading a CTI/Kudu session, which means the funk has a second-line looseness that the New York studio records lack.
listenFor: Muhammad's snare placement is slightly behind the grid throughout — the New Orleans feel inside a mid-1970s studio production.

title: Dancing in Your Head
label: A&M Horizon
whyThisOne: Prime Time's arrival. Two guitars, electric bass and drums playing a hard groove while a simple, repeated melody is bent in every direction on top. Also includes Coleman playing with Moroccan musicians in Joujouka.
listenFor: The tune is one short phrase, repeated for over twenty minutes. Everything else — five people playing melody simultaneously — happens around and against it.

title: Of Human Feelings
label: Antilles
whyThisOne: Prime Time fully formed: doubled guitars, doubled basses, doubled drummers, and one of the first jazz records recorded digitally. Harmolodics as a working band language rather than a theory.
listenFor: There is no accompanist. Every instrument is playing a melodic line, and the groove emerges from six independent melodies happening to coincide rhythmically.

title: Tales of Captain Black
label: Artists House
whyThisOne: Ulmer's debut with Coleman as sideman, and the clearest recording of harmolodic guitar. His tuning and attack have no obvious ancestor in either jazz or blues guitar.
listenFor: Ulmer tunes his guitar so that all the strings are related to one pitch, which makes chords ambiguous by design. Nothing sounds like it is in a key.

artist: Ronald Shannon Jackson and the Decoding Society
title: Eye on You
label: About Time
whyThisOne: Jackson had played with Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor and Albert Ayler, and the Decoding Society is what he built out of all three plus Texas funk. Vernon Reid is on guitar, years before Living Colour.
listenFor: Jackson's drumming is a second-line New Orleans feel underneath free playing. He grew up in Fort Worth and it shows in every bar.

title: Song X
label: Geffen
whyThisOne: A guitarist with a huge mainstream audience made a Coleman record on a rock label and did not soften it. It confused Metheny's listeners and introduced harmolodics to a lot of them anyway.
listenFor: Metheny's guitar synth is used for noise and texture rather than for melody. He is not visiting the idiom politely.

title: Show Stopper
label: Gramavision
whyThisOne: Prime Time's bassist as a leader, treating electric bass as a lead melodic voice with a bright, trebly tone that nobody else used. The writing is funkier and more song-shaped than Coleman's.
listenFor: The bass is mixed as the lead instrument and plays in the upper register throughout. The bottom end is being handled by the kick drum alone.

title: Last Exit
label: Enemy
whyThisOne: European free jazz, harmolodic drums, noise guitar and a producer's bass, playing at metal volume with no material prepared at all. It is the loudest music in this guide.
listenFor: Nothing is composed. Four musicians with completely different backgrounds improvising at maximum volume, and it coheres — barely, and on purpose.

artist: Ronald Shannon Jackson and the Decoding Society
title: Mandance
label: Antilles
whyThisOne: Jackson's compositions at their most intricate, with written horn lines over grooves in unusual meters. It is more composed than most free funk and consequently harder to play.
listenFor: The horn writing is in unison and very fast, over a groove that keeps shifting its subdivision. The band has to be right together or the whole thing collapses.

title: Ask the Ages
label: Axiom
whyThisOne: Sharrock's last major record, produced by Bill Laswell, with Pharoah Sanders and Elvin Jones. It is a Coltrane-quartet record with an electric guitarist in Coltrane's chair, and it works.
listenFor: Sharrock plays with sustained feedback and slide as melodic devices. Elvin Jones plays exactly as he did in 1965 and the two languages fit.

title: Winelight
label: Elektra
whyThisOne: The record that defined the format, made by a musician who could genuinely play. 'Just the Two of Us' with Bill Withers was a top-three single and the album won two Grammys.
listenFor: Marcus Miller's bass playing is far more interesting than the format requires. Underneath the gloss there is a serious rhythm section doing careful work.

title: Street Life
label: MCA
whyThisOne: The Jazz Crusaders were a hard bop band in 1961; by 1979 they had dropped the 'Jazz' and had a hit single with a vocalist. The whole crossover arc is visible in one group's discography.
listenFor: Wilton Felder's tenor still phrases like a hard bop player. The arrangement around him has changed completely and he has not.

title: Breezin'
label: Warner Bros.
whyThisOne: The first jazz album to be certified platinum, made by a guitarist who had been Jack McDuff's sideman at nineteen. It is where a formidable bebop player chose the crossover route deliberately.
listenFor: Benson sings in unison with his guitar solos, an octave apart. It became a signature and it is technically much harder than it sounds.

title: Voyeur
label: Warner Bros.
whyThisOne: Sanborn's alto tone — piercing, blues-derived, instantly identifiable — became the most imitated sound in the format. This is the record where it locked into place.
listenFor: The tone comes from playing rhythm and blues behind singers, not from Charlie Parker. It is a different lineage and the intensity in it is real.

title: Morning Dance
label: Infinity
whyThisOne: The commercial template in its purest form: a steel-drum hook, an unvarying mid-tempo groove and a saxophone melody you cannot dislodge. It sold over a million copies.
listenFor: Nothing is at stake at any point, by design. Hearing what has been engineered out is more informative than hearing what is there.

title: Breathless
label: Arista
whyThisOne: One of the best-selling instrumental albums in history and the record that made 'smooth jazz' an insult. It belongs here because pretending it does not exist explains nothing about how the genre worked.
listenFor: The melodies are written to be memorable on one hearing and the improvisation is minimal. Whatever else it is, it is expertly built for its purpose.

title: A Day in the Life
label: A&M/CTI
whyThisOne: Creed Taylor put one of the great jazz guitarists in front of a string orchestra playing Beatles covers, and it sold. This is the ancestral form of the smooth jazz proposition.
listenFor: Montgomery's octave technique and thumb-picked tone are entirely intact; the setting around them is pop. The argument about whether that is a compromise starts here.

title: One on One
label: Tappan Zee/Columbia
whyThisOne: Nylon-string guitar and electric piano as a duo-led format, which is the most chamber-like the genre gets. It won a Grammy and set the acoustic-guitar wing of the format going.
listenFor: Klugh plays fingerstyle nylon-string, a classical technique, in a pop-funk setting. The combination is more unusual than it sounds now.

title: Still Life (Talking)
label: Geffen
whyThisOne: The most musically ambitious record that regularly gets shelved next to smooth jazz, which says something about how blunt the category is. Brazilian rhythm, wordless vocals and genuinely complex writing.
listenFor: 'Last Train Home' has an ostinato that never stops and a melody that arrives late and leaves early. It is doing what smooth jazz does and doing it with real compositional care.

title: The Brand New Heavies
label: Acid Jazz
whyThisOne: The scene's best band playing original material rather than pastiche, with a rhythm section tight enough to pass for 1973. It is the most listenable entry point to a movement that was often more about curation than composition.
listenFor: The drums and bass are recorded dry and up-front in the 1970s manner, with no 1990s reverb. The production is as much a period reference as the playing.

title: Positivity
label: Talkin' Loud
whyThisOne: Bluey Maunick's writing is the most durable in the idiom — actual songs rather than grooves with a topline — and this is the record where the band's own material outgrew its influences.
listenFor: The horn arrangements and the layered backing vocals are doing the work of a much bigger band. It is a studio construction with live playing at its core.

title: Hand on the Torch
label: Blue Note
whyThisOne: Blue Note gave a British production duo unrestricted access to its master tapes, and the result was the label's first platinum record. It is the clearest case of the sampled and the sampling generations sharing a contract.
listenFor: 'Cantaloop' is built on Herbie Hancock's 'Cantaloupe Island' from Empyrean Isles, with a live trumpet playing over the loop. Both records are in this guide.

title: Mission Impossible
label: Re-Elect the President
whyThisOne: Hammond organ instrumentals covering TV themes, released before 'acid jazz' had a name. It is the scene's rawest and most literal reconstruction of 1960s soul jazz.
listenFor: There is essentially no improvisation. It is a groove band playing arrangements, which is what most of acid jazz actually was.

title: The Return of the Space Cowboy
label: Sony Soho Square
whyThisOne: The most commercially enormous thing acid jazz produced, and the second album is where the band's playing caught up with its ambition. Stuart Zender's bass is the reason it holds up.
listenFor: The bass lines are genuinely difficult and carry the harmonic content. Strip the vocals and this is a jazz-funk instrumental band.

title: A Joyful Noise Unto the Creator
label: Talkin' Loud
whyThisOne: The first act signed to Talkin' Loud, combining spoken-word and rap with live jazz-funk and an explicitly spiritual bent. It is closer to the Last Poets than to a dance record.
listenFor: The rapping is British, unhurried and consciously not American in cadence — one of the earliest examples of a UK voice in this space.

title: Rebirth of Cool Volume One
label: 4th & Broadway
personnel: compiled by Gilles Peterson and Norman Jay
whyThisOne: The compilation series that defined the sensibility, mixing hip-hop, jazz, dub and soul with no regard for genre boundaries. It shows acid jazz as a listening position rather than a sound.
listenFor: The sequencing is the argument. Records that had no relationship to each other are placed side by side until a common thread becomes audible.

title: Out of Here
label: Acid Jazz
whyThisOne: The mod end of the scene — Hammond-driven, sharp-suited, and closer to 1960s British R&B than to American soul jazz. It documents acid jazz as a British subculture rather than a revival.
listenFor: The organ sound and the arrangements come from Georgie Fame and Brian Auger rather than from Jimmy Smith. The lineage is local.
note: Acid Jazz label catalogue numbering from this period is inconsistently documented; details should be verified.

title: Wake Up
label: Ichiban
whyThisOne: The living ancestor recording during the acid jazz years and being adopted by the scene that had rediscovered him. Ayers toured with these bands and the traffic was genuinely two-way.
listenFor: The production is late-1980s and the playing is unchanged from 1976. Hearing the mismatch clarifies what the revival was and was not reproducing.
note: Ayers' late-1980s discography on small labels is patchily documented; verify before citing.

title: The Low End Theory
label: Jive
whyThisOne: The record that proved jazz samples and rapping were not a novelty pairing. Sparse, bass-forward, and with Ron Carter playing upright on one track at Q-Tip's request.
listenFor: There is almost nothing in the mix — a bass line, drums, one sample, two voices. The restraint is what makes the low end sound so enormous.

title: Daily Operation
label: Chrysalis
whyThisOne: DJ Premier's chopping technique at its sharpest — samples cut into fragments and reassembled rather than looped whole. Guru's flat, unhurried delivery is a rhythmic instrument in itself.
listenFor: Premier takes half a second of a jazz record and repitches it across a bar. The source is often unrecognisable, which is the point: he is composing, not quoting.

title: Reachin' (A New Refutation of Time and Space)
label: Pendulum
whyThisOne: The most explicitly jazz-referencing rap record of the era, down to the personas and the Art Blakey samples. It won a Grammy and made the aesthetic briefly mainstream.
listenFor: 'Rebirth of Slick' is built on a loop from Art Blakey's 'Stretchin''. The upright bass and the brushed drums are doing the same job they did in 1958.

title: Jazzmatazz, Volume 1
label: Chrysalis
whyThisOne: The first sustained attempt to put live jazz musicians and a rapper in a studio together rather than sampling them. Donald Byrd, Roy Ayers and Lonnie Liston Smith — the men whose records had been sampled — playing in person.
listenFor: The difference between a sampled loop and a live rhythm section is immediately audible, and not always in the live section's favour. That tension is the record's subject.

title: Mecca and the Soul Brother
label: Elektra
whyThisOne: The richest horn-sample production of the era, built from soul jazz and hard bop records layered several deep. 'They Reminisce Over You' is an elegy built from a Tom Scott saxophone figure.
listenFor: Pete Rock stacks multiple horn samples so the result sounds like a section that never existed. It is arranging by other means.

title: Black Radio
label: Blue Note
whyThisOne: A jazz pianist made an R&B and hip-hop record with a jazz band's interactivity, and it won a Grammy. It established the template that most of the current jazz-adjacent mainstream works from.
listenFor: Chris Dave's drumming is the whole argument — an acoustic kit playing with the timing displacement of a programmed Dilla beat, live.

title: Shades of Blue
label: Blue Note
whyThisOne: Blue Note handed a producer its vaults for a second time, and Madlib both remixed the originals and re-recorded material himself playing every instrument. It is a producer's reading of a catalogue.
listenFor: Some tracks are remixes and some are Madlib playing all the parts under a false band name. Working out which is which is genuinely difficult.

title: Doo-Bop
label: Warner Bros.
whyThisOne: Davis's last album, unfinished at his death and completed by producer Easy Mo Bee from existing trumpet takes. It is not good, and it is historically unavoidable — the last thing he chose to chase was hip-hop.
listenFor: The trumpet playing is recognisably Davis and the production around it was assembled without him. The seam is audible and worth hearing.

title: Do You Want More?!!!??!
label: DGC
whyThisOne: A rap group with no samples at all, playing everything live, with Cassandra Wilson and Steve Coleman guesting. It inverts the whole jazz rap premise — instead of sampling jazz, they play it.
listenFor: Questlove's drumming reproduces the feel of a sampled loop on an acoustic kit, deliberately imperfect. This is where the technique that Chris Dave later refined begins.

title: Khmer
label: ECM
whyThisOne: ECM's trumpet lyricism placed over drum programming and dub bass, and the record that made electronic jazz a European proposition rather than a novelty. It sold far beyond the label's usual reach.
listenFor: The trumpet is played sparsely and drenched in delay, so a single note becomes a texture. The electronics are not accompaniment — they are the composition.

title: New Conception of Jazz
label: Jazzland
whyThisOne: The record that named the Norwegian project and launched the Jazzland label. Wesseltoft treats the sequencer as a bandmate rather than a backing track, which is the whole difference.
listenFor: The programmed elements are deliberately allowed to drift and the live players adjust to them. Nothing is locked to a click.

title: Tourist
label: Blue Note
whyThisOne: Deep house grooves with live jazz soloing and blues samples, released on Blue Note and selling over two million copies. It is the commercial peak of the whole idea.
listenFor: 'Rose Rouge' loops a Marlena Shaw vocal phrase over a house beat while a live trumpet solos across it. Three eras of Black American music, stacked.

title: Motion
label: Ninja Tune
whyThisOne: Sampled and looped material with live improvisation on top, made for a label built on hip-hop production. It is the British answer to the Norwegian project, arrived at independently.
listenFor: The loops are treated as chord changes to solo over. The saxophone is doing exactly what a jazz soloist does, just over a producer's structure.

title: A Livingroom Hush
label: Smalltown Supersound
whyThisOne: A ten-piece Norwegian band writing for horns, vibraphone, tuba and electronics as one integrated machine. It is the most compositionally ambitious thing nu jazz produced.
listenFor: The arrangements are intricate and largely written, with electronics woven into the ensemble rather than layered on top. This is a big band that grew up on Autechre.

title: In Between
label: JCR/Sonar Kollektiv
whyThisOne: The Berlin production team's first album, connecting broken beat, Brazilian material, soul vocals and jazz harmony into something coherent. It is the European production wing at its most assured.
listenFor: The rhythms are broken beat — displaced, syncopated, never quite settling — and the harmony underneath is straightforwardly jazz. That combination is the genre's core.

title: Électronique Noire
label: Jazzland
whyThisOne: Molvær's guitarist as a leader, using the guitar as a sound-design instrument rather than a solo voice. It is more abstract than Khmer and better for it.
listenFor: There are almost no identifiable guitar sounds. Everything is processed into pads, textures and rhythmic pulses, and the improvisation happens at the level of timbre.

title: Two Pages
label: Talkin' Loud
whyThisOne: Drum and bass producers making a double album with a string orchestra, jazz harmony and spoken word. It is the record where the London electronic scene stopped pretending it was not making jazz.
listenFor: The strings are arranged, not sampled, and the drum programming runs at 170 BPM underneath ballad-tempo melodies. Two time-feels at once.

title: Waltz for Koop
label: JCR/Compost
whyThisOne: A Swedish duo who built tracks entirely from tiny samples of acoustic jazz records — a single note at a time — and reassembled them into new arrangements. The method is extreme and inaudible.
listenFor: It sounds like a live jazz band and almost none of it is. Every note was sampled separately from old records and sequenced.

title: The Epic
label: Brainfeeder
whyThisOne: Three hours, seventeen tracks, choir and strings, released on an electronic label and reaching an audience that had not been listening to jazz. The 1970s spiritual jazz ambition returns without a hint of irony.
listenFor: Two drummers play throughout, panned left and right, playing different parts. The choir functions as an orchestral section, not as a garnish.

title: Cosmogramma
label: Warp
whyThisOne: The record where the beat scene reached explicitly for jazz — harp, Ravi Coltrane on saxophone, and a structure closer to a suite than to a beat tape. Flying Lotus is Alice Coltrane's great-nephew and the reference is deliberate.
listenFor: The harp is a direct citation of Alice Coltrane, and the way tracks bleed into one another without pause is a suite structure imported from 1970s Impulse! records.

title: Drunk
label: Brainfeeder
whyThisOne: Twenty-three tracks, most under two minutes, with bass playing of real virtuosity underneath deadpan songs about cats and video games. The fusion lineage is worn openly, including hiring Michael McDonald.
listenFor: The bass playing is technically extraordinary and mixed like a pop record. Stanley Clarke and Jaco Pastorius are the ancestors and Thundercat has said so directly.

title: To Pimp a Butterfly
label: Top Dawg/Aftermath/Interscope
whyThisOne: A mainstream rap album made with a live jazz band, and the record that put the whole West Coast Get Down in front of a global audience. It is where the scene became visible.
listenFor: 'For Free?' is a jazz interlude at bebop tempo with rapping over the top. The band is playing changes and Lamar is phrasing against them.

title: Velvet Portraits
label: Ropeadope
whyThisOne: The producer-musician who assembled the To Pimp a Butterfly sessions making his own record, which is more explicitly jazz than anything he produced for others.
listenFor: The vocoder is used as a horn section, layered in harmony. It is a G-funk device deployed with jazz voicing.

title: Universal Beings
label: International Anthem
whyThisOne: McCraven records live improvisation and then edits it into composed tracks in the manner of a hip-hop producer. Four sessions in four cities, including London with Shabaka Hutchings and Nubya Garcia.
listenFor: The tracks are cut from long improvisations, so a groove will be interrupted and resumed in a way live playing never does. The edit is the composition.

title: Suite for Ma Dukes: The Music of James Yancey
label: Mochilla
whyThisOne: J Dilla's beats orchestrated for a forty-piece ensemble, which forced someone to work out what the harmony in those tracks actually was. It is the clearest evidence that the beats were compositions.
listenFor: The orchestration reveals harmonic movement that the original short loops only implied. Dilla's chord choices turn out to be far from simple.

title: Suite for Max Brown
label: International Anthem / Nonesuch
whyThisOne: Tortoise's guitarist building a record from his own sampled loops, played mostly by himself, with jazz players dropping in. It is the beat aesthetic applied by someone from the post-rock side.
listenFor: Parker samples himself, loops it, and then plays over the loop. The 'band' on much of this is one person assembled in layers.

title: The Return
label: Black Focus
whyThisOne: The London counterpart to the LA scene, built on broken beat and jazz-funk keyboards rather than on spiritual jazz. It shows the two cities working the same territory from different directions.
listenFor: The drums have the same off-grid feel as the LA records but derive it from UK garage and broken beat rather than from Dilla directly.

title: The Köln Concert
label: ECM
whyThisOne: The best-selling solo piano album ever made, improvised in one sitting on a badly out-of-tune house piano that Jarrett nearly refused to play. He worked around the instrument's faults and the record is shaped by them.
listenFor: He avoids the piano's weak upper register and dead pedals by staying in the middle and using ostinatos. The limitation produced the style.

title: Afric Pepperbird
label: ECM
whyThisOne: ECM's Nordic wing at its most aggressive, before the label's reputation for beauty set in. This is free jazz played by Norwegians who had studied with George Russell, and it is closer to Ayler than to Garbarek's later sound.
listenFor: The tone is already unmistakable — cold, pure, huge — but the playing is far more violent than what Garbarek became known for a decade later.

title: Belonging
label: ECM
whyThisOne: Jarrett's 'European quartet', with tunes that are folk-simple and playing that is anything but. It is the most perfectly balanced record either Jarrett or Garbarek made.
listenFor: 'Long as You Know You're Living Yours' is a two-chord vamp with a melody a child could sing, and the band builds twenty minutes of tension out of refusing to resolve it.
startTrack: Long as You Know You're Living Yours

title: The Colours of Chloë
label: ECM
whyThisOne: Weber built his own five-string electric upright bass and wrote chamber music for it. The record's sound — enormous, singing, sustained bass over cellos — has no antecedent.
listenFor: The bass carries the melody for long stretches with a sustain and pitch clarity that an acoustic bass cannot produce. The instrument is the composition's premise.

title: Bright Size Life
label: ECM
whyThisOne: Metheny at twenty-one with Jaco Pastorius, in a trio with no chordal instrument other than the guitar. It brought an American, country-inflected lyricism into ECM's world.
listenFor: The guitar tone is clean and reverberant with almost no attack, which became one of the most imitated sounds in jazz. Pastorius is playing melody as much as bass.

title: Litania: The Music of Krzysztof Komeda
label: ECM
whyThisOne: Stańko playing the music of Krzysztof Komeda, the Polish composer and Polanski's film scorer, in whose band he had played as a young man. It is a distinctly Central European strand of the label's aesthetic.
listenFor: Komeda's melodies are dark and song-like in a way that Nordic material is not — the harmonic language comes from Polish film music, not Norwegian folk.

title: Odyssey
label: ECM
whyThisOne: Sustained, distorted, orchestral electric guitar inside ECM's acoustic world. Rypdal plays long held notes rather than lines, closer to a string section than to a rock guitarist.
listenFor: He almost never plays fast. The guitar produces slowly evolving sustained tones, and the volume pedal removes every attack.

title: Tales of Another
label: ECM
whyThisOne: Nominally Peacock's record, this is the first meeting of the trio that Jarrett later led for thirty years. The interplay is already fully formed and the writing is Peacock's, which changes the character.
listenFor: Peacock's compositions are more angular than Jarrett's, and the trio treats them more freely than it treated standards later. A different band under the same name.

title: Goodbye
label: ECM
whyThisOne: The Swedish pianist with Paul Motian, playing material from Ornette Coleman to Cuban song to Alban Berg. It is the label's chamber aesthetic at its most patient and least sentimental.
listenFor: Motian's drumming has no timekeeping function at all — he is playing colour and shape, and the trio finds the pulse collectively or not at all.
